title: Comparative connectomics reveals stage-specific gap junction rewiring that reshapes avoidance behavior
authors: Choe, D. T.; Hall, D. H.; Nguyen, K. C. Q.; Choi, M.; Bae, J. A.; Lee, J.
abstract: Environmental stress can remodel neural circuits, yet how such rewiring generates behavioral adaptation remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated how dauer-specific circuit remodeling alters nociceptive behavior. We discovered that dauers exhibit significantly shorter avoidance durations than adults. Through comparative connectomics, we observed a substantial expansion of gap junctions within the dauer nociceptive circuit and found that dauer neurons exhibit more transient activity dynamics as a result of this rewiring. Modeling neuronal activity demonstrated that removing dauer-specific connectivity constraints failed to reproduce transient characteristics, validating the functional role of dauer-specific gap junctions. Furthermore, introducing synthetic dauer-specific gap junctions into adults was sufficient to recapitulate dauer-like activity patterns and shorten avoidance duration. Despite extensive rewiring, avoidance initiation remained preserved across developmental stages. Our findings show that the dauer neural circuit is selectively rewired through gap junction remodeling to balance flexibility and stability for survival under stress.

title: The nucleus spatially partitions mechanoprotection and mechanosensing
authors: Bouzignac, R.; Palandri, A.; Fritsch, L.; Merle, T.; Zine el Aabidine, A.; Mangeat, T.; Gracia, M.; Andrieu, C.; Garcia Idieder, P.; Trullo, A.; Cazales, M.; Marques Prieto, S.; Pimmett, V.; Costes, M.; Rouviere, C.; Lagha, M. L.; Suzanne, M.
abstract: Mechanical forces shape cell behavior, but how the nucleus integrates its roles as genome protector and mechanosensor remains unresolved. Here, we dissect the spatiotemporal control of transcriptional response to forces during epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT). By combining genome-wide approaches, in vivo nuclear micromanipulation, and quantitative live imaging, we uncover two key properties of nuclear mechanosensing. First, mechanically induced changes in chromatin accessibility and transcription are spatially patterned within the nucleus: genes closest to deformations appear protected, revealing a local shielding mechanism associated with chromatin closure. Second, relocating a gene between chromatin environments is sufficient to alter its mechanosensitivity, challenging the concept of inherently force-sensitive genes. These findings demonstrate unexpected spatial partition of nuclear response to forces.

title: Integrating Long-Read Structural Variant Analysis with single-nucleus RNA-seq to Elucidate Gene Expression Effects in Disease
authors: Kim, K.; Lin, Z.; Simmons, S. K.; Parker, J.; Kearney, M.; Liao, Z.; Haywood, N.; Zhang, J.; Cline, M. P.; Tuncali, I.; Sharma, M.; Serrano, G. E.; Beach, T. G.; Dong, X.; Popic, V.; Scherzer, C. R.; Levin, J. Z.
abstract: Structural variants (SVs) are a major source of genetic diversity, yet how they impact cell types in complex brain diseases remains largely unexplored, partially due to limitations of short-read sequencing. Here, we addressed this fundamental question in Parkinson's disease (PD). generating long-read whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data for 100 post-mortem brain samples from a PD cohort, constructing a high-confidence catalog of 74,552 SVs. To resolve their functional impact, we integrated single-nucleus RNA-sequencing data from two brain regions from the same samples and focused functional analyses on SVs proximal to genes previously nominated as cis-regulated, potential causal targets of PD-associated GWAS loci. Using expression quantitative trait locus and allele-specific expression analyses, we uncovered SVs significantly associated with expression in specific cell types as well as effects shared across cell types. This study demonstrates the power of uniting long-read WGS with transcriptomics to uncover SVs underlying complex disease architecture with cell type resolution.

title: A reformulation of the t-test in single-cell transcriptomics dramatically reduces false positives
authors: Kviman, O.; Ferreira, P. F.; Jun, S.-H.; Toosi, H.; Lagergren, J.
abstract: The default differential expression tests in single-cell analysis software provide fast and simple approaches that help practitioners annotate cell populations identified through clustering algorithms. Here, we use theoretical arguments and empirical studies to show that these tests suffer from inflated false positive rates that affect the resulting annotations. We introduce LN's t-test, which tests a novel, asymptotically unbiased log-fold change estimator and avoids these false positives, without compromising speed.

title: Modulating inter-mitochondrial contacts to increase membrane potential for mitigating blue light damage
authors: Wang, Y.; Qiu, K.; Zou, W.; Amom, P.; Ganjawala, T.; Lee, E.; Tian, Z.; Xu, X.; Huang, T.; Tsai, N.-P.; Shi, D.; Kang, P.; Bai, H.; Zacharias, A. L.; Zhang, K.; Diao, J.
abstract: Mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) is essential for mitochondrial functions, yet current methods for modulating MMP lack precise spatial and temporal control. Here, we developed an optogenetic mitochondrial tethering system, termed OptoMitoTether, that enables reversible control of inter-mitochondrial proximity with high spatiotemporal precision. Blue light activation induced CRY2PHR oligomerization between adjacent mitochondrial outer membranes, reduced mitochondrial nearest-neighbor distances, and promoted inter-mitochondrial tethering. OptoMitoTether activation was associated with elevated MMP and was associated with lower reactive oxygen species (ROS) and preserved ATP production during prolonged blue light stress. Moreover, OptoMitoTether expression preserved mitochondrial bioenergetic function in human retinal cells and extended lifespan in C. elegans during chronic blue light exposure. These findings establish OptoMitoTether as a tool for manipulating mitochondrial proximity and reveal a link between inter-mitochondrial tethering and mitochondrial bioenergetic state during blue light stress.

title: Temporal Dynamics of Multi-Item Working Memory Maintenance in Human Gaze Patterns and EEG
authors: Broehl, F.; Bielefeldt, A. A.; Linde-Domingo, J.; Spitzer, B.
abstract: Maintaining multiple items in working memory (WM) requires the allocation of limited resources, which may involve prioritizing individual items over others. Previous work has suggested that attentional prioritization can vary rhythmically between WM samples, but direct empirical evidence for such temporal fluctuations remains scarce. Here, we recorded eye-tracking and EEG to track the temporal dynamics of multi-item processing while participants maintained up to three object orientations in WM. Whereas EEG encoding was only short-lived, miniature gaze patterns reflected the orientations of all three items throughout the entire WM delay and showed systematic load and serial position effects. Contrary to rhythmic sampling accounts, however, we found no evidence that eye movements alternated between the concurrently maintained items. Furthermore, the strength of WM encoding in gaze was not modulated by frontal theta activity in EEG, suggesting that oculomotor encoding was not directly coupled to rhythmic neural dynamics associated with WM and internal attention. Together, our findings indicate that the oculomotor signature of visuospatial WM processing was rather stably shaped by all of the simultaneously maintained items. The results further corroborate that eye-tracking and EEG provide complementary windows into the temporal dynamics of WM.

title: OpenDrive: An Open-Source Microdrive for Large-Scale Neurophysiology
authors: Stine, G. M.; Gabel, J.; Watters, N.; Jazayeri, M.
abstract: Neuropixels-NHP probes have ushered in a new era of high-density neurophysiology recording in large animal models. Here, we present OpenDrive, an open-source microdrive system designed specifically for acute insertion of Neuropixels-NHPs. OpenDrive combines a custom motorized microdrive, six-drive control console, and software platform. Compared with commercially available options, OpenDrive offers (1) low cost, (2) precise, accurate, and stable probe movement, (3) scalability to many-probe recording, and (4) open-source hardware designs and software. In our experiments, OpenDrive has already supported recordings from thousands of neurons across a variety of cortical and subcortical structures. By lowering technical barriers and enabling community-driven development with OpenDrive, we aim to accelerate Neuropixels recording in large animal models.

title: A nanoscale atlas of extracellular vesicles and particles in Drosophila olfactory sensilla
authors: Vijayakumar, P.; Cauwenberghs, K.; Garg, M.; Choy, J.; Charara, S.; McKaughan, Q.; Su, C.-Y.
abstract: Extracellular particles, including non-vesicular extracellular particles (NVEPs) and extracellular vesicles (EVs), are emerging as key contributors to sensory signaling, yet their ultrastructural organization within native tissues remains underexplored. Native tissues preserve extracellular particle organization and heterogeneity that are often lost during dissociation. Using cryofixation-based serial block-face scanning electron microscopy, we generated a nanoscale atlas of NVEPs and EVs across 352 Drosophila antennal olfactory sensilla ([~]70% coverage). Segmentation of more than 7,800 extracellular particles revealed distinct populations differing in morphology, size, electron density, and sensillum-class distribution. Analyses of EV biogenesis identified multivesicular bodies and membrane budding in auxiliary cells. Furthermore, sensilla housing degenerating neurons exhibited marked accumulation of EVs and NVEPs, accompanied by increased auxiliary-cell EV biogenesis. Together, these findings provide a large-scale ultrastructural characterization of extracellular particles in native sensory tissues and establish a foundation for understanding how extracellular particles are distributed, generated, and function during sensory signaling and degeneration.

title: WHaloForce enables chemigenetic imaging of molecular tension in living cells and animals
authors: Wu, D.; Morales, E. A.; Lee, J.; Pangeni, S.; Farrants, H.; Hutchings, K. A.; Barndt, R. J.; Yu, Q.; Li, X.; Shroff, H.; Wu, H.; Tebo, A. G.; Lavis, L. D.; Schreiter, E. R.; Ha, T.; Wang, S.
abstract: Piconewton forces borne by individual proteins within complex assemblies underlie cell adhesion, migration, and tissue morphogenesis, yet remain difficult to image in living systems. Here, we introduce WHaloForce, a chemigenetic HaloTag-based tension sensor that converts force-dependent relief of tryptophan-mediated dye quenching into a fluorescence lifetime change. Optical tweezers revealed a switch-like unquenching transition near 5 pN, and cellular measurements demonstrated dynamic responses to actomyosin activity. WHaloForce enabled quantitative tension imaging of diverse force-bearing proteins (vinculin, E-cadherin, -catenin, and laminin) in mammalian cells, mouse tissue, and C. elegans. Bright synthetic dyes made tension measurements possible at endogenous expression levels. In C. elegans, vinculin and laminin showed opposite tension patterns between tissues, highlighting tissue-specific force transmission through adhesions and the extracellular matrix. We also identified ovulation as a source of molecular loading within the spermathecal laminin network. WHaloForce thus offers a modular platform for imaging spatiotemporal tension patterns in living systems.

title: Replicative and chronological epigenetic age track genome instability in opposite directions across cancers
abstract: Epigenetic clocks are widely applied to tumor tissue, yet clocks trained to predict chronological age and clocks built to count cell divisions measure different quantities, and how either relates to the heterogeneity of methylation change within a tumor remains unclear. Here we compare four mitotic clocks with Horvath pan tissue clock in 506 matched tumor and normal pairs from 13 adult solid cancers and in 1,731 pediatric tumors. We show that mitotic age is higher in the tumor than in matched normal tissue in every adult cancer type, and that this advance is robust to tumor purity and cell type composition. The advance is explained chiefly by global methylation change and cell composition, with tumor proliferation contributing a small component that generalises across cancer types only for stemTOC; beyond proliferation, mitotic clock advance is associated with tumor grade, stage and genome instability, whereas Horvath clock is not, or is inversely so. Horvath clock, by contrast, reads older in renal clear cell and thyroid tumors and younger in endometrial, lung squamous, head and neck and prostate tumors, while in children 98.1% of tumors return a Horvath age above chronological age. Neither clock family is associated, patient by patient, with the heterogeneity of methylation change once its global magnitude and purity are accounted for, and neither changes consistently between primary and relapse. Methylation change is enriched on the X chromosome in female tumors only, independently of X copy number. Our data indicate that replicative epigenetic age is near uniformly advanced in cancer and records tissue remodelling more than current proliferation, whereas chronological clock readings of tumors are specific to cancer type and do not report clonal diversification in bulk tissue.

title: Programmable amide bond formation using de novo ligases
authors: Salike, S.; Fluegel, T.; Gantz, M.; Moroz, S. S.; Hunt, A. C.; Jones, H.; Singh, A.; Corley, N.; Didi, K.; Brent, R. I.; Kazman, M. W.; Xu, Z.; Savvides, C.; Woodbury, S. M.; Sotomayor, B.; Nguyen, H.; Mendoza, J.; Kang, A.; Bera, A. K.; Li, X.; Banala, S.; Butcher, J.; Lavis, L. D.; Green, A. P.; Hilvert, D.; Baker, D.
abstract: Amide bond formation is of central importance in the chemical industry, underpinning the synthesis of small bioactive molecules, macrocycles, peptides and their conjugates. Conventional methods of amide synthesis rely on stoichiometric coupling agents and costly protecting group manipulations. While biocatalysis can alleviate some of these challenges, enzymes typically operate across a narrow range of substrates and their adaptation to new coupling partners requires extensive engineering. Here we show that de novo amide ligases featuring a cysteine catalytic triad can be programmed computationally to operate across diverse substrate classes with high selectivity. We first designed complementary peptide ligases to selectively functionalise either the N-terminus or a single lysine residue of a polypeptide sequence containing 36 competing lysines. Crystal structures of both ligases show excellent agreement with the designs, with structural modelling suggesting that amidation outcompetes hydrolysis because the catalytically competent geometry forms only upon acceptor binding. We then extended our approach to the synthesis of small bioactive molecules by designing stereoselective ligases that mediate a key amide bonding forming step in the synthesis of the preventative HIV therapeutic lenacapavir. These results establish de novo enzyme design as a programmable platform for achieving selective amide bond formations across a wide range of molecular targets.

title: SIFT: Syncmer-Informed Selection of Haplotypes for T2T Imputation
authors: Ferro, E. A.; Varki, R.; Lin, M.-J.; Gagie, T.; Langmead, B.; Boucher, C. A.
abstract: Genome patching improves the completeness of fragmented assemblies by filling unresolved gaps with sequences from reference genomes. Pangenome panels provide diverse candidate haplotypes for this task, but identifying suitable references efficiently becomes increasingly challenging as these panels grow. We present SIFT, a compressed indexing method for selecting reference haplotypes for genome patching with ImpuT2T. SIFT combines closed-syncmer parsing, phrase-level indexing, and pseudo-maximal exact match (pseudo-MEM) queries. Closed syncmers provide a context-independent parsing rule with bounded distances between consecutive selected positions, enabling consistent parsing of reference and query sequences. We demonstrate that two closed syncmers determine the distance at which they can occur consecutively in any string, so that equal substrings of two parses represent identical sequences and no gap sequence need be stored. SIFT indexes the reference parse and its reverse using run-length compressed suffix arrays and adapts the Boyer-Moore-Li search procedure to identify pseudo-MEMs between the reference parse and query parse. It then aggregates matching evidence to identify candidate reference haplotypes for downstream patching. This framework connects compressed sequence indexing with haplotype selection and provides a basis for querying large reference panels at the phrase level. SIFT is publicly available under the GNU license at https://github.com/EddieFerro/SIFT.

title: Assessing the Capacity of Genomic Language Models to Generate Informative Embeddings of Viral Genome Fragments
authors: Kladchenko, A.; Manolov, A.; Popov, N. S.
abstract: Genomic language models (gLMs) trained on large volumes of nucleotide sequences are becoming an alternative to classical methods in metagenomic analysis, particularly for studying genomic "dark matter". In this work, we investigate the ability of four gLMs (DNABERT-2, DNABERT-S, ViraLM, and Evo2-7B) to generate taxonomically informative vector representations of short viral genome fragments. We constructed a balanced reference dataset of viruses based on the ICTV Virus Metadata Resource and compared the representations generated by gLMs with conventional k-mer profiles and MinHash sketches using clustering and neighborhood-based metrics (adjusted Rand index (ARI), precision@k, and CROSS precision@k). On the reference dataset, three of the four gLMs outperformed the 4-mer profile in terms of ARI and precision@5 under the same evaluation protocol. The best performance was generally achieved by intermediate model layers. Conventional k-mer profiles consistently outperformed MinHash sketches. We further evaluated the methods on two viral orders (egoviruses and mriyaviruses) absent from the reference dataset, with model layers and k-mer lengths selected exclusively on the reference dataset. DNABERT-S showed the most consistently strong performance across these two orders, ranking first on mriyaviruses and second on egoviruses, while k-mer profiles with Jensen-Shannon distance remained competitive. We also observed the consistency of representations between forward fragments and their reverse complements. Overall, the best-performing gLMs surpassed conventional baselines, although their advantage depended on the dataset and evaluation metric. The consistently strong performance of DNABERT-S suggests a potential benefit of contrastive fine-tuning and indicates that larger models are not necessarily more effective for generating taxonomically informative representations.

title: zsasa: a Zig-based engine for high-throughput solvent accessible surface area at proteome scale
abstract: Advances in structural and computational biology now yield structures by the hundreds of thousands, from predicted-structure databases to molecular-dynamics trajectories. Solvent accessible surface area (SASA), a long-established descriptor of protein stability, binding, and interfaces, remains central to their analysis. Established SASA tools are still widely used, but each covers only part of what such data now demand in input formats, outputs, and speed. We present zsasa, a fast, full-featured, open-source SASA engine for single structures, proteome-scale collections, and trajectories, usable from the command line or Python. It uses the same algorithms as established tools and owes its speed to the implementation, which makes full use of multicore processors and SIMD instructions while keeping memory use low. On a single laptop, zsasa reproduced FreeSASA, a widely used SASA library, down to individual atom areas on 4,370 Escherichia coli AlphaFold models. On the 23,586 structures of the human AlphaFold proteome, it was 3.3-fold faster than FreeSASA run in parallel while using a third or less of the peak memory of the other tools tested, and an optional approximate mode was 10-fold faster, with total SASA within 0.7% of the default results on average. On molecular-dynamics trajectories, it was 12- to 52-fold faster than MDTraj. As a demonstration, we computed interface burial for more than 600,000 predicted human protein dimers in under half an hour and found that a large buried area did not imply a confident predicted interface. zsasa is available under the MIT license at https://github.com/N283T/zsasa.
